snapshot.title: TNPSC History: Sangam Age & Culture
snapshot.exam_hook: 🎯 TNPSC Tamil/History Hook: 5 Thinais. Chola: Tiger. Chera: Bow. Pandya: Fish. Ettuthokai: 8 books. Pattuppattu: 10 books. Keezhadi: Sangam urban civilization.

quick_notes.title: The 3 Sangams (தமிழ் சங்கங்கள்)
quick_notes.detail: 1. Mudhal Sangam (Old Madurai). 2. Idai Sangam (Kapatapuram). 3. Kadai Sangam (Modern Madurai). Kadai Sangam literature is what survives today.
quick_notes.explanation: The 3 Sangams, also called Tamil Sangams, were ancient academies or gatherings of Tamil poets and scholars who created and preserved Tamil literature. The first Sangam, called Mudhal Sangam, was held in Old Madurai and was attended by gods and legendary sages, but all its works are lost. The second Sangam, called Idai Sangam, was held in Kapatapuram, a city that was later destroyed by a flood, and none of its literature survives today. The third Sangam, called Kadai Sangam, was held in Modern Madurai and was sponsored by the Pandya kings, and its literature is the only Sangam literature that still exists. The surviving Kadai Sangam works include famous collections like the Ettuthokai (Eight Anthologies) and the Pathupattu (Ten Idylls), which are the oldest known Tamil poems. These poems describe the life, love, war, and nature of ancient Tamil people, and they are the main source for understanding the Sangam period.

quick_notes.title: The 5 Thinais (ஐந்திணை)
quick_notes.detail: Classification of landscape: 1. Kurinji (Mountains). 2. Mullai (Forest). 3. Marutham (Agricultural). 4. Neithal (Coastal). 5. Paalai (Desert). Each has its own deity, people, and occupation.
quick_notes.explanation: The 5 Thinais, also called the Five Landscapes, is an ancient Tamil system that divides the natural world into five types of land. The first is Kurinji, which means mountains and hills, where people worship the god Murugan and work as hunters or gatherers. The second is Mullai, meaning forests and grasslands, where the deity is Thirumal and people live as herders of cattle. The third is Marutham, which is agricultural land with fields and farms, where the god is Indra and people work as farmers growing crops like rice. The fourth is Neithal, meaning coastal areas near the sea, where the deity is Varuna and people make a living by fishing and collecting salt. The fifth is Paalai, which is the desert or dry wasteland, where the goddess is Kali and people survive as travelers or bandits in harsh conditions.

quick_notes.title: Pathinen Melkanakku (Major 18)
quick_notes.detail: Comprises Ettuthokai (8 Anthologies) and Pattuppattu (10 Idyls). Examples : Purananuru (History/Bravery), Akananuru (Love), Maduraikanchi.
quick_notes.explanation: Pathinen Melkanakku, which means the Major 18, is a collection of eighteen ancient Tamil poems. This collection is divided into two main parts: Ettuthokai, which means the Eight Anthologies, and Pattuppattu, which means the Ten Idyls. The Eight Anthologies include works like Purananuru, which is a poem about history and bravery, and Akananuru, which is a poem about love. The Ten Idyls include works like Maduraikanchi, which describes the city of Madurai and its king. These poems were written by different poets and are some of the oldest surviving examples of Tamil literature. They give us information about the society, culture, and rulers of ancient Tamilakam, the region where Tamil was spoken.

quick_notes.title: The 3 Great Kingdoms (மூவேந்தர்)
quick_notes.detail: Cheras (Vanji, Palm flower, Bow & Arrow symbol). Cholas (Uraiyur, Atthi flower (Aatthi / Bauhinia), Tiger symbol, Karikala Chola). Pandyas (Madurai, Neem flower, Fish symbol, Pearl trade).
quick_notes.explanation: The 3 Great Kingdoms, called Moovendhar in Tamil, were three powerful ruling families in ancient Tamilakam, which is the old name for the Tamil-speaking region of South India. The Cheras ruled from their capital Vanji, used the palm flower as their emblem, and their royal symbol was a bow and arrow. The Cholas ruled from their capital Uraiyur, used the atthi flower, also called Bauhinia, as their emblem, had the tiger as their royal symbol, and a famous early king was Karikala Chola. The Pandyas ruled from their capital Madurai, used the neem flower as their emblem, had the fish as their royal symbol, and were well-known for trading pearls.

quick_notes.title: Sangam Society
quick_notes.detail: Women were respected (Avvaiyar). Trade with Rome (Arikamedu). Hero stones (Nadukal) for fallen soldiers. Religious diversity (Murugan, Indra, Vishnu).
quick_notes.explanation: Sangam Society refers to the people and culture of ancient South India, as described in Tamil poems written between 300 BCE and 300 CE. Women in this society were respected and could be poets, like the famous poet Avvaiyar. The region had active trade with the Roman Empire, with archaeological evidence found at Arikamedu, a port town in present-day Puducherry. When a soldier died in battle, people erected a hero stone, called a Nadukal, to honor his bravery. The society practiced religious diversity, meaning they worshipped many different gods, including Murugan (the Tamil war god), Indra (the king of gods in Vedic religion), and Vishnu (the preserver god in Hinduism).

lesson_intro: Today we travel back 2000 years to the 'Golden Age' of Tamil culture—The Sangam Period. This was the time of the three great academies (Sangams) in Madurai, where thousands of poets composed masterpieces that still define Tamil identity today. We explore the 'Thinai' system—the classification of land into 5 types—and the literature of 'Ettuthokai' and 'Pattuppattu'. For a TNPSC aspirant, this is the most high-yield history block. Understanding how the Cheras, Cholas, and Pandyas lived is the key to mastering Unit 8.
